question: A pathology slide shows cardiac muscle fibers with prominent intercalated discs and lipofuscin pigment in the cytoplasm. Which layer of the heart is primarily represented in this section?
cited_learning_objective: Review normal cardiac histology (AACOM competencies 1.2.d, Il.1.f; Course goal mapping 1, 3, 6)

options.text: Epicardium layer containing mesothelium and adipose tissue
options.rationale: Wrong because epicardium is the visceral pericardium with mesothelium and adipose; the slide describes abundant myocytes and intercalated discs which are not epicardial features. It would be correct if the slide showed mesothelial cells and subepicardial fat.

options.text: Endocardium layer lined by endothelium and subendocardial tissue
options.rationale: Wrong because endocardium is endothelial-lined with subendocardial connective tissue; intercalated discs and lipofuscin are myocardial features. It would be correct if the slide emphasized endothelial lining and elastic fibers.

options.text: Myocardium composed predominantly of cardiac muscle fibers
options.rationale: Correct because the myocardium is the muscular wall containing cardiac myocytes with intercalated discs and age-related lipofuscin, matching the described histology.

options.text: Parietal pericardium with dense fibrous outer layer
options.rationale: Wrong because parietal pericardium is fibrous and not composed of cardiac muscle; the slide shows muscle features. It would be correct if the section showed dense fibrous tissue and mesothelial surface.

options.text: Subepicardial connective tissue layer with coronary vessels
options.rationale: Wrong because subepicardial connective tissue contains vessels and fat but not the organized cardiac myocytes with intercalated discs; it would be correct if the slide highlighted vessels and adipose rather than myocytes.

question: Which morphologic pattern of cardiomyopathy is characterized by global chamber enlargement with systolic dysfunction and frequent mural thrombi formation?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the 3 morphologic/functional patterns of cardiomyopathies (AACOM competencies I.2.d, II.1.f; Course goal mapping 1, 3, 6)

options.text: Dilated cardiomyopathy with four chamber dilation and systolic failure
options.rationale: Correct because dilated cardiomyopathy shows progressive dilation of chambers, systolic dysfunction, and predisposition to mural thrombi as described in the lecture.

options.text: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with asymmetric septal thickening and diastolic dysfunction
options.rationale: Wrong because hypertrophic cardiomyopathy features massive hypertrophy and diastolic impairment rather than global dilation and mural thrombi; it would be correct if the stem described septal hypertrophy and outflow obstruction.

options.text: Restrictive cardiomyopathy with decreased ventricular compliance and diastolic filling defect
options.rationale: Wrong because restrictive cardiomyopathy causes impaired compliance and diastolic dysfunction without the global dilation and frequent mural thrombi typical of dilated cardiomyopathy; it would be correct if the stem emphasized infiltration or fibrosis limiting filling.

options.text: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy with focal RV wall thinning and fatty replacement
options.rationale: Wrong because ARVC primarily affects the right ventricle with fibrofatty replacement and arrhythmias, not global chamber dilation with systolic failure and mural thrombi; it would be correct if the stem focused on RV arrhythmias and adipose replacement.

options.text: Constrictive pericarditis causing external restriction of ventricular filling
options.rationale: Wrong because constrictive pericarditis is an external pericardial process limiting filling and is not a myocardial dilation with systolic dysfunction; it would be correct if the stem described pericardial thickening and calcification.

question: A 28-year-old patient with a family history of sudden cardiac death has asymmetric septal thickening and myocyte disarray on biopsy. Which molecular defect most likely explains this phenotype?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiologies of each type of cardiomyopathy (AACOM competencies I.2.d, II.1.f; Course goal mapping 1, 3, 6)

options.text: Mutation in beta-myosin heavy chain affecting sarcomeric function
options.rationale: Correct because hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is commonly due to autosomal dominant mutations in sarcomeric proteins such as beta-myosin heavy chain, producing myocyte hypercontractility and disarray as described in the lecture.

options.text: Truncating mutation in titin leading to impaired passive elasticity
options.rationale: Wrong because TTN truncating mutations are classically associated with dilated cardiomyopathy rather than asymmetric septal hypertrophy; it would be correct if the phenotype were global dilation and systolic dysfunction.

options.text: Dystrophin gene deletion causing defective membrane cytoskeleton coupling
options.rationale: Wrong because dystrophin mutations are linked to X-linked dilated cardiomyopathy and skeletal myopathies, not primary sarcomeric hypertrophy with myocyte disarray; it would be correct if the patient had dilated ventricles and skeletal muscle weakness.

options.text: Mitochondrial DNA deletion causing impaired fatty acid oxidation in myocardium
options.rationale: Wrong because mitochondrial defects more often present with energy transfer problems and can cause various cardiomyopathies but are not the classic cause of asymmetric septal hypertrophy with sarcomeric disarray; it would be correct if there were multisystem mitochondrial features and early-onset disease.

options.text: Mutation in desmosomal plakoglobin causing fibrofatty replacement of myocardium
options.rationale: Wrong because desmosomal protein mutations cause arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy with fibrofatty replacement, not hypertrophic asymmetric septal hypertrophy; it would be correct if the presentation involved RV arrhythmias and adipose replacement.

question: Which histologic feature is most characteristic of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and helps distinguish it from physiologic athletic hypertrophy?
cited_learning_objective: Visually recognize and describe the characteristic gross and histologic findings of each type of cardiomyopathy (AACOM competencies I.2.d, Il.1.f; Course goal mapping 1, 3, 6)

options.text: Myocyte disarray with interstitial fibrosis on microscopic examination
options.rationale: Correct because hypertrophic cardiomyopathy shows myocyte/myofiber disarray and interstitial fibrosis, distinguishing it from physiologic hypertrophy which lacks disarray and fibrosis.

options.text: Uniform concentric myocyte hypertrophy without fibrosis
options.rationale: Wrong because uniform concentric hypertrophy without fibrosis is more typical of adaptive hypertrophy (e.g., hypertension) rather than the disarray seen in HCM; it would be correct if the lecture described pressure overload concentric changes without disarray.

options.text: Extensive subendocardial collagen deposition with iron deposition
options.rationale: Wrong because iron deposition and subendocardial scarring are features seen in other conditions like hemochromatosis or ischemia-related injury, not the hallmark myocyte disarray of HCM; it would be correct if Prussian blue stain showed iron overload.

options.text: Diffuse adipose replacement of ventricular myocardium
options.rationale: Wrong because diffuse adipose replacement is characteristic of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, not hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; it would be correct if the slide showed focal adipose replacement of RV myocardium.

options.text: Endocardial fibroelastosis with thickened elastic layer
options.rationale: Wrong because endocardial fibroelastosis is an endocardial process seen in infants and restrictive physiology, not the myocyte disarray and hypertrophy of HCM; it would be correct if the pathology emphasized endocardial elastic thickening.

question: A patient with chronic alcohol abuse presents with progressive dyspnea and an enlarged, flabby heart on imaging. Which pathophysiologic mechanism best explains the reduced ejection fraction in this condition?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the 3 morphologic/functional patterns of cardiomyopathies (AACOM competencies I.2.d, II.1.f; Course goal mapping 1, 3, 6)

options.text: Impaired myocardial contractility due to myocyte injury and dilation
options.rationale: Correct because dilated cardiomyopathy from toxins like alcohol causes myocyte injury, chamber dilation, and systolic dysfunction leading to reduced ejection fraction as described in the lecture.

options.text: Decreased ventricular compliance from interstitial amyloid deposition
options.rationale: Wrong because decreased compliance from amyloid causes restrictive physiology and diastolic dysfunction rather than the systolic impairment and dilation seen with alcohol-related DCM; it would be correct if the patient had restrictive filling patterns and amyloid infiltration.

options.text: Obstruction of outflow tract from asymmetric septal hypertrophy
options.rationale: Wrong because outflow obstruction from asymmetric septal hypertrophy causes preserved systolic function with diastolic filling impairment, not the reduced ejection fraction and global dilation seen in alcoholic cardiomyopathy; it would be correct if the exam showed systolic anterior motion and LVOT gradient.

options.text: External pericardial constriction limiting diastolic filling and stroke volume
options.rationale: Wrong because constrictive pericarditis limits filling externally and causes diastolic dysfunction without primary systolic failure and chamber dilation; it would be correct if pericardial thickening and calcification were present.

options.text: Coronary artery occlusion causing regional wall motion abnormality
options.rationale: Wrong because ischemic CAD causes regional systolic dysfunction and infarct-related remodeling rather than the global dilation and diffuse systolic impairment typical of nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy; it would be correct if there were focal infarct and coronary occlusion evidence.

question: Which genetic inheritance pattern and common mutated gene are most associated with familial dilated cardiomyopathy described in the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiologies of each type of cardiomyopathy (AACOM competencies I.2.d, II.1.f; Course goal mapping 1, 3, 6)

options.text: Autosomal dominant inheritance with TTN gene truncating mutations
options.rationale: Correct because familial dilated cardiomyopathy is often autosomal dominant and truncating mutations in TTN (titin) account for a significant proportion of cases as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Autosomal recessive inheritance with beta-myosin heavy chain mutations
options.rationale: Wrong because beta-myosin heavy chain mutations are classically linked to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and the inheritance is typically autosomal dominant, not autosomal recessive; it would be correct if the phenotype were HCM with dominant transmission.

options.text: X-linked inheritance with myosin-binding protein C mutations
options.rationale: Wrong because myosin-binding protein C mutations are associated with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and are usually autosomal dominant, not X-linked; it would be correct if the lecture described X-linked dystrophin-related cardiomyopathy.

options.text: Mitochondrial inheritance with desmosomal protein mutations
options.rationale: Wrong because desmosomal protein mutations cause arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy and are not mitochondrial; mitochondrial inheritance would be implicated if multisystem energy defects were present.

options.text: Autosomal dominant inheritance with dystrophin gene deletions
options.rationale: Wrong because dystrophin gene deletions are X-linked and associated with Duchenne/Becker muscular dystrophies and dilated cardiomyopathy in males, not autosomal dominant; it would be correct if the pedigree showed X-linked transmission and skeletal muscle disease.

question: A young athlete collapses during exercise and is found to have ventricular arrhythmia. Autopsy reveals focal thinning of the right ventricular wall with fibrofatty replacement. Which molecular defect best matches this finding?
cited_learning_objective: Brief discussion of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy

options.text: Mutation in desmosomal junction proteins such as plakoglobin
options.rationale: Correct because arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy is linked to mutations in desmosomal proteins (e.g., plakoglobin) leading to fibrofatty replacement of RV myocardium and arrhythmias as described in the lecture.

options.text: Truncating titin mutation causing global ventricular dilation
options.rationale: Wrong because titin truncating mutations cause dilated cardiomyopathy with global dilation rather than focal RV fibrofatty replacement; it would be correct if the heart showed four-chamber dilation and systolic dysfunction.

options.text: Sarcomeric beta-myosin heavy chain mutation causing septal hypertrophy
options.rationale: Wrong because beta-myosin heavy chain mutations cause hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with septal hypertrophy and myocyte disarray, not RV fibrofatty replacement; it would be correct if asymmetric septal hypertrophy were present.

options.text: Dystrophin deficiency causing X-linked dilated cardiomyopathy
options.rationale: Wrong because dystrophin deficiency leads to X-linked dilated cardiomyopathy and skeletal myopathy, not focal RV fibrofatty replacement and arrhythmias typical of ARVC; it would be correct if there were progressive dilation and skeletal muscle disease.

options.text: Mitochondrial tRNA mutation causing diffuse myocardial fibrosis
options.rationale: Wrong because mitochondrial tRNA mutations cause multisystem energy defects and can produce diffuse cardiomyopathy but not the focal fibrofatty RV replacement characteristic of ARVC; it would be correct if systemic mitochondrial features were present.

question: Which clinical finding is most consistent with hypertrophic obstructive physiology caused by asymmetric septal thickening?
cited_learning_objective: Visually recognize and describe the characteristic gross and histologic findings of each type of cardiomyopathy (AACOM competencies I.2.d, Il.1.f; Course goal mapping 1, 3, 6)

options.text: Harsh systolic ejection murmur with exertional syncope
options.rationale: Correct because asymmetric septal hypertrophy causing LV outflow tract obstruction produces a harsh systolic ejection murmur and can cause exertional syncope as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Low-pitched diastolic rumble and wide pulse pressure
options.rationale: Wrong because a low-pitched diastolic rumble and wide pulse pressure suggest valvular regurgitation or high-output states, not LVOT obstruction from septal hypertrophy; it would be correct if there were severe aortic regurgitation.

options.text: S3 gallop with peripheral edema and hepatomegaly
options.rationale: Wrong because S3 gallop with peripheral edema and hepatomegaly is more typical of dilated cardiomyopathy with systolic failure, not the hypercontractile, diastolic dysfunction of HCM; it would be correct if the patient had reduced LVEF and volume overload.

options.text: Kussmaul sign with elevated jugular venous pressure on inspiration
options.rationale: Wrong because Kussmaul sign is associated with constrictive pericarditis or restrictive cardiomyopathy, not asymmetric septal hypertrophy causing LVOT obstruction; it would be correct if pericardial constriction were present.

options.text: Pulsus paradoxus with marked inspiratory blood pressure drop
options.rationale: Wrong because pulsus paradoxus is seen in tamponade and severe asthma, not in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy; it would be correct if there were pericardial tamponade causing inspiratory BP drop.

question: Which of the following causes is included in the mnemonic ABCCCD for dilated cardiomyopathy etiologies as presented in the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiologies of each type of cardiomyopathy (AACOM competencies I.2.d, II.1.f; Course goal mapping 1, 3, 6)

options.text: Alcohol abuse as a toxic cause of myocardial dysfunction
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture lists alcohol abuse as one of the causes in the ABCCCD mnemonic for dilated cardiomyopathy etiologies.

options.text: Amyloid deposition causing restrictive ventricular filling
options.rationale: Wrong because amyloidosis is a cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy, not part of the ABCCCD causes for dilated cardiomyopathy; it would be correct if the question asked about restrictive etiologies.

options.text: Aortic stenosis producing concentric hypertrophy and outflow obstruction
options.rationale: Wrong because aortic stenosis causes secondary hypertrophic changes and is not listed in the ABCCCD mnemonic for primary dilated cardiomyopathy causes; it would be correct if the stem described secondary myocardial dysfunction from valvular disease.

options.text: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy causing RV fibrofatty change
options.rationale: Wrong because ARVC is a distinct variant and not one of the ABCCCD toxic or infectious causes for dilated cardiomyopathy; it would be correct if the question targeted ARVC features.

options.text: Hypertensive heart disease causing concentric left ventricular hypertrophy
options.rationale: Wrong because hypertensive heart disease is a secondary myocardial dysfunction that can mimic cardiomyopathy but is not part of the ABCCCD list of primary dilated cardiomyopathy causes; it would be correct if the stem asked about secondary causes mimicking cardiomyopathy.

question: A biopsy from a patient with suspected hemochromatosis-related cardiomyopathy is stained with Prussian blue. What finding would confirm iron overload in the myocardium?
cited_learning_objective: Visually recognize and describe the characteristic gross and histologic findings of each type of cardiomyopathy (AACOM competencies I.2.d, Il.1.f; Course goal mapping 1, 3, 6)

options.text: Blue granular deposits within myocytes on Prussian blue stain
options.rationale: Correct because Prussian blue stain highlights iron as blue granules within myocytes, confirming iron overload as noted in the lecture's discussion of hemochromatosis in DCM.

options.text: Extensive collagen staining blue on Masson trichrome stain
options.rationale: Wrong because Masson trichrome stains collagen blue, indicating fibrosis, not iron; it would be correct if the question asked about interstitial fibrosis rather than iron deposition.

options.text: Lipid vacuoles within myocytes on Oil Red O stain
options.rationale: Wrong because Oil Red O stains neutral lipids and would indicate fatty change, not iron overload; it would be correct if the pathology showed fatty infiltration such as in ARVC.

options.text: Yellow-brown lipofuscin pigment in cytoplasm on H&E stain
options.rationale: Wrong because lipofuscin is a wear-and-tear pigment seen with aging and stains differently, not the blue iron granules detected by Prussian blue; it would be correct if the stem emphasized age-related pigment accumulation.

options.text: Focal adipose replacement of myocardium on H&E stain
options.rationale: Wrong because focal adipose replacement suggests arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, not iron overload; it would be correct if the biopsy showed fibrofatty replacement of RV myocardium.

question: Which clinical management step is most appropriate as initial therapy for a patient with symptomatic hypertrophic obstructive physiology to reduce outflow gradient and symptoms?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the key clinical and histologic features of cardiac amyloidosis, endomyocardial fibrosis, Loeffler endomyocarditis, and endocardial fibroelastosis (AACOM competencies I.2.d, II.1.f; Course goal mapping 1, 3, 6)

options.text: Initiate beta-adrenergic blockade to reduce heart rate and contractility
options.rationale: Correct because beta-blockers reduce heart rate and contractility, decreasing LVOT gradient and symptoms in hypertrophic obstructive physiology as recommended in the lecture's treatment section for HCM.

options.text: Begin high-dose loop diuretics to reduce preload and relieve obstruction
options.rationale: Wrong because reducing preload with aggressive diuresis can worsen LVOT obstruction in HCM; it would be correct if the patient had volume overload without dynamic obstruction and careful monitoring.

options.text: Administer intravenous inotropic agents to improve systolic function
options.rationale: Wrong because inotropes increase contractility and can exacerbate LVOT obstruction in hypertrophic obstructive physiology; it would be correct if the patient had true systolic failure without obstruction.

options.text: Urgent percutaneous coronary intervention to relieve ischemia
options.rationale: Wrong because PCI addresses coronary occlusion and is not the initial therapy for dynamic LVOT obstruction due to HCM; it would be correct if there were acute coronary occlusion causing ischemia.

options.text: Immediate surgical myomectomy without medical therapy trial
options.rationale: Wrong because surgical septal reduction is reserved for refractory cases after medical therapy; it would be correct if the patient remained symptomatic despite optimal medical management.

question: A 45-year-old woman in the peripartum period develops progressive dyspnea and an LVEF of 30%. Which lecture-listed etiology best explains her presentation?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiologies of each type of cardiomyopathy (AACOM competencies I.2.d, II.1.f; Course goal mapping 1, 3, 6)

options.text: Peripartum cardiomyopathy presenting as nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy
options.rationale: Correct because peripartum cardiomyopathy is a recognized cause of dilated cardiomyopathy with reduced LVEF occurring in the peripartum period as listed in the lecture.

options.text: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy due to sarcomeric mutation manifesting postpartum
options.rationale: Wrong because HCM is genetic and presents with hypertrophy and preserved systolic function, not new-onset reduced LVEF in the peripartum period; it would be correct if there were septal hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction.

options.text: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy causing left ventricular failure
options.rationale: Wrong because ARVC primarily affects the right ventricle with fibrofatty replacement and arrhythmias, not typical peripartum LV systolic failure; it would be correct if RV fibrofatty change and arrhythmias predominated.

options.text: Restrictive cardiomyopathy from amyloid deposition presenting acutely postpartum
options.rationale: Wrong because amyloid-related restrictive cardiomyopathy is an infiltrative chronic process causing diastolic dysfunction, not acute peripartum systolic failure; it would be correct if biopsy showed amyloid infiltration.

options.text: Ischemic cardiomyopathy from coronary atherosclerosis causing reduced LVEF
options.rationale: Wrong because ischemic cardiomyopathy is secondary to CAD and would require evidence of coronary disease; it would be correct if coronary angiography showed obstructive lesions causing infarction.

question: Which gross heart description best matches the typical appearance of dilated cardiomyopathy at autopsy?
cited_learning_objective: Visually recognize and describe the characteristic gross and histologic findings of each type of cardiomyopathy (AACOM competencies I.2.d, Il.1.f; Course goal mapping 1, 3, 6)

options.text: Enlarged heavy heart with flabby globular chambers and mural thrombi
options.rationale: Correct because dilated cardiomyopathy produces an enlarged, heavy, flabby heart with chamber dilation and a propensity for mural thrombi as described in the lecture.

options.text: Massively thickened ventricular wall with small left ventricular cavity
options.rationale: Wrong because that description fits hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with concentric or asymmetric hypertrophy, not dilated cardiomyopathy; it would be correct if the heart showed septal bulging and small LV cavity.

options.text: Right ventricular wall thinning with focal adipose replacement
options.rationale: Wrong because RV wall thinning with adipose replacement is characteristic of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, not the global dilation of DCM; it would be correct if the pathology focused on RV fibrofatty change.

options.text: Rigid noncompliant ventricles with endocardial thickening
options.rationale: Wrong because rigid noncompliant ventricles and endocardial thickening suggest restrictive cardiomyopathy or endocardial fibroelastosis, not the flabby dilation of DCM; it would be correct if the ventricles were stiff and poorly compliant.

options.text: Pericardial sac thickening with calcification and constriction
options.rationale: Wrong because pericardial thickening and calcification describe constrictive pericarditis, an external cause of diastolic dysfunction, not intrinsic dilated cardiomyopathy; it would be correct if pericardial pathology were present.

question: A biopsy shows focal transmural replacement of right ventricular myocardium by adipose tissue and fibrosis. Which clinical consequence is most directly explained by this pathology?
cited_learning_objective: Brief discussion of arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy

options.text: Ventricular arrhythmias leading to sudden cardiac death in young patients
options.rationale: Correct because fibrofatty replacement of RV myocardium disrupts conduction and predisposes to ventricular arrhythmias and sudden death, a key clinical feature of ARVC described in the lecture.

options.text: Progressive left ventricular outflow obstruction with syncope
options.rationale: Wrong because LVOT obstruction with syncope is a feature of hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy, not focal RV fibrofatty replacement; it would be correct if asymmetric septal hypertrophy were present.

options.text: Marked systemic embolization from left ventricular mural thrombi
options.rationale: Wrong because mural thrombi and systemic embolization are more typical of dilated cardiomyopathy with LV dilation and stasis, not focal RV fibrofatty replacement; it would be correct if LV dilation and thrombus were present.

options.text: Diastolic heart failure from diffuse myocardial amyloid infiltration
options.rationale: Wrong because diastolic failure from amyloid is a restrictive process involving diffuse infiltration, not focal fibrofatty RV replacement; it would be correct if Congo red staining showed amyloid.

options.text: Acute coronary syndrome from transmural ischemic necrosis
options.rationale: Wrong because transmural ischemic necrosis from coronary occlusion causes infarction, not the chronic fibrofatty replacement seen in ARVC; it would be correct if there were evidence of coronary thrombosis and acute infarct.

question: Which diagnostic feature on imaging or exam would help distinguish dilated cardiomyopathy from hypertrophic cardiomyopathy?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the 3 morphologic/functional patterns of cardiomyopathies (AACOM competencies I.2.d, II.1.f; Course goal mapping 1, 3, 6)

options.text: Reduced left ventricular ejection fraction with chamber dilation on echocardiogram
options.rationale: Correct because dilated cardiomyopathy is characterized by reduced LVEF ( 80% is not a typical finding in cardiomyopathies and would suggest hyperdynamic states, not dilated cardiomyopathy; it would be correct only in rare hypercontractile conditions.

options.text: Left ventricular ejection fraction exactly equal to 50 percent
options.rationale: Wrong because an LVEF of 50% is within normal to mildly reduced range and does not specifically indicate dilated cardiomyopathy which usually has EF <40%; it would be correct if the patient had borderline systolic function.

question: A patient with suspected myocarditis from Coxsackie B virus later develops progressive ventricular dilation and systolic dysfunction. According to the lecture, this sequence most commonly leads to which cardiomyopathy phenotype?
cited_learning_objective: Discuss the etiologies of each type of cardiomyopathy (AACOM competencies I.2.d, II.1.f; Course goal mapping 1, 3, 6)

options.text: Dilated cardiomyopathy as a late complication of viral myocarditis
options.rationale: Correct because viral myocarditis (e.g., Coxsackie B) can lead to chronic myocardial injury, progressive dilation, and systolic dysfunction characteristic of dilated cardiomyopathy as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy from viral-induced sarcomeric mutation
options.rationale: Wrong because viral myocarditis does not induce sarcomeric mutations causing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; it would be correct only if a genetic sarcomeric mutation were present.

options.text: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy from viral desmosomal damage
options.rationale: Wrong because ARVC is primarily genetic due to desmosomal mutations, not a typical sequela of Coxsackie B myocarditis; it would be correct if desmosomal gene mutations were identified.

options.text: Restrictive cardiomyopathy from viral amyloid deposition
options.rationale: Wrong because viral infections do not typically cause amyloid deposition leading to restrictive cardiomyopathy; it would be correct if amyloid infiltration were documented.

options.text: Constrictive pericarditis from viral pericardial scarring
options.rationale: Wrong because constrictive pericarditis is an external pericardial process and while viral pericarditis can rarely lead to constriction, the lecture emphasizes myocarditis leading to dilated cardiomyopathy rather than pericardial constriction.

question: Which histologic change is described in the lecture as a nonspecific finding in dilated cardiomyopathy biopsies?
cited_learning_objective: Visually recognize and describe the characteristic gross and histologic findings of each type of cardiomyopathy (AACOM competencies I.2.d, Il.1.f; Course goal mapping 1, 3, 6)

options.text: Myocyte hypertrophy with interstitial fibrosis as nonspecific features
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture notes that dilated cardiomyopathy often shows nonspecific myocyte hypertrophy and interstitial fibrosis on histology.

options.text: Myocyte disarray with marked hypertrophy as pathognomonic features
options.rationale: Wrong because myocyte disarray is characteristic of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, not a nonspecific finding in dilated cardiomyopathy; it would be correct if HCM were being described.

options.text: Transmural adipose replacement of myocardium as a common finding
options.rationale: Wrong because transmural adipose replacement is typical of ARVC, not a nonspecific feature of DCM; it would be correct if ARVC pathology were present.

options.text: Extensive amyloid deposition in interstitium as a routine finding
options.rationale: Wrong because amyloid deposition is specific for amyloidosis-related restrictive cardiomyopathy, not a routine nonspecific finding in DCM; it would be correct if Congo red positive deposits were identified.

options.text: Marked endocardial elastic thickening in adult hearts
options.rationale: Wrong because marked endocardial elastic thickening describes endocardial fibroelastosis typically in infants, not a nonspecific adult DCM finding; it would be correct if infantile endocardial disease were present.

question: A patient with suspected restrictive cardiomyopathy has pulmonary hypertension and left atrial enlargement. Which pathophysiologic sequence from the lecture best explains these findings?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the 3 morphologic/functional patterns of cardiomyopathies (AACOM competencies I.2.d, II.1.f; Course goal mapping 1, 3, 6)

options.text: Decreased ventricular compliance leading to elevated left atrial pressure and pulmonary hypertension
options.rationale: Correct because restrictive cardiomyopathy causes impaired ventricular filling and decreased compliance, raising left atrial pressure and producing pulmonary hypertension and atrial enlargement as described in the lecture.

options.text: Primary pulmonary vascular disease causing secondary left atrial enlargement
options.rationale: Wrong because primary pulmonary vascular disease elevates right-sided pressures and may secondarily affect the left atrium indirectly, but the lecture emphasizes intrinsic ventricular compliance defects causing left atrial hypertension in restrictive cardiomyopathy; it would be correct if primary pulmonary vascular pathology were documented.

options.text: Global systolic failure causing left atrial enlargement from volume overload
options.rationale: Wrong because global systolic failure (DCM) leads to volume overload and dilation but the mechanism for pulmonary hypertension and LA enlargement in restrictive cardiomyopathy is impaired filling and elevated filling pressures, not primary systolic failure; it would be correct if LVEF were markedly reduced.

options.text: Obstructive coronary artery disease causing ischemic mitral regurgitation and atrial dilation
options.rationale: Wrong because ischemic MR can cause LA enlargement and pulmonary hypertension, but the lecture's restrictive cardiomyopathy mechanism is decreased compliance leading to elevated filling pressures; it would be correct if severe ischemic MR were present.

options.text: Pericardial constriction causing increased left atrial pressure and pulmonary hypertension
options.rationale: Wrong because pericardial constriction can mimic restrictive physiology and cause elevated filling pressures, but the lecture specifically lists intrinsic myocardial restrictive causes; it would be correct if pericardial thickening and constriction were demonstrated.

question: Which of the following is a lecture-listed distinguishing gross configuration described as 'banana-shaped' and what does it indicate?
cited_learning_objective: Visually recognize and describe the characteristic gross and histologic findings of each type of cardiomyopathy (AACOM competencies I.2.d, Il.1.f; Course goal mapping 1, 3, 6)

options.text: Bulging ventricular septum into the lumen indicating asymmetric septal hypertrophy
options.rationale: Correct because the 'banana-shaped' ventricular configuration results from septal bulging into the LV cavity due to asymmetric septal hypertrophy in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy as described in the lecture.

options.text: Globular dilated heart indicating four-chamber dilation in DCM
options.rationale: Wrong because a globular dilated heart describes dilated cardiomyopathy, not the banana-shaped septal bulge of HCM; it would be correct if the heart were flabby and enlarged.

options.text: Transmural adipose replacement indicating ARVC
options.rationale: Wrong because transmural adipose replacement is a feature of ARVC and does not produce a banana-shaped LV configuration; it would be correct if RV fibrofatty replacement were the focus.

options.text: Concentric thickening producing small cavity in pressure overload
options.rationale: Wrong because concentric hypertrophy from pressure overload produces a small cavity but is not the banana-shaped septal bulge specific to asymmetric HCM; it would be correct if concentric hypertrophy were present.

options.text: Endocardial plaque formation causing localized outflow obstruction
options.rationale: Wrong because endocardial plaque formation may occur with systolic anterior motion of the mitral leaflet in HCM but does not itself define the banana-shaped ventricular configuration; it would be correct if the question emphasized endocardial plaques in the outflow tract.

question: Which lecture-described patient population is most commonly affected by hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and when does it typically present?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the 3 morphologic/functional patterns of cardiomyopathies (AACOM competencies I.2.d, II.1.f; Course goal mapping 1, 3, 6)

options.text: Typically presents during postpubertal growth spurt often in adolescents and young adults
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture notes HCM may present at any age but typically during the postpubertal growth spurt, often in adolescents and young adults.

options.text: Usually presents in late adulthood after decades of hypertension
options.rationale: Wrong because late adulthood presentation after chronic hypertension is more typical of hypertensive heart disease causing secondary hypertrophy, not primary genetic HCM which often presents earlier; it would be correct if the hypertrophy were secondary to long-standing hypertension.

options.text: Exclusively presents in infancy with endocardial fibroelastosis
options.rationale: Wrong because endocardial fibroelastosis presents in infancy, but HCM typically presents later during adolescence or young adulthood; it would be correct if the pathology were infantile endocardial disease.

options.text: Only occurs in middle-aged athletes with repetitive high-intensity training
options.rationale: Wrong because HCM is genetic and not caused solely by athletic training; athlete's heart is a physiologic adaptation and differs histologically from HCM; it would be correct if physiologic hypertrophy without disarray were present.

options.text: Commonly presents in neonates with congenital structural defects
options.rationale: Wrong because neonatal presentation with congenital defects is not the typical pattern for primary HCM, which often manifests later; it would be correct if congenital syndromes causing early hypertrophy were present.

question: Which lecture-described therapeutic agent is mentioned as an option for refractory hypertrophic cardiomyopathy to reduce hypercontractility at the sarcomere level?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the key clinical and histologic features of cardiac amyloidosis, endomyocardial fibrosis, Loeffler endomyocarditis, and endocardial fibroelastosis (AACOM competencies I.2.d, II.1.f; Course goal mapping 1, 3, 6)

options.text: Mavacamten as a targeted agent to reduce sarcomeric hypercontractility
options.rationale: Correct because the lecture mentions mavacamten as a therapy for refractory HCM that reduces sarcomeric hypercontractility and can alleviate obstruction.

options.text: High-dose beta-agonists to increase contractile force and relieve obstruction
options.rationale: Wrong because beta-agonists increase contractility and would worsen LVOT obstruction in HCM; it would be correct only if the goal were to treat systolic failure without obstruction.

options.text: Intravenous iron chelation to reduce myocardial iron and improve compliance
options.rationale: Wrong because iron chelation treats hemochromatosis-related cardiomyopathy, not sarcomeric hypercontractility in HCM; it would be correct if iron overload were documented.

options.text: Aldosterone receptor antagonists to reduce septal hypertrophy directly
options.rationale: Wrong because aldosterone antagonists reduce remodeling and fibrosis but are not targeted sarcomeric inhibitors like mavacamten; it would be correct if the therapy aimed at reducing fibrosis in heart failure.

options.text: Calcium channel blockers to increase heart rate and contractility
options.rationale: Wrong because nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers reduce heart rate and contractility and are used in HCM, but they do not specifically target sarcomeric hypercontractility at the molecular level like mavacamten; it would be correct if the question asked about rate control rather than targeted sarcomeric therapy.
